If you have the space to keep two vehicles, getting a second used car is a good option, assuming you take your time to find a fair deal on it. When you are reliant on your vehicle for your income, you need to be continuously socking away a portion of your earnings to pay for preventative maintenance and so that if something goes wrong you have all funds available to immediately get it repaired.

Those car-shield type programs are a ripoff imo. Car maintenance is predictable enough that it's basically just a car maintenance sayings account where you pay somebody else to hold your money in case you need it, except you don't get the money back if you cancel the service or get rid of the car before you end up needing it.

I like to think about vehicles by fractions of their usable lifetime.

When they're 1/3 used up (by age and miles, let's assume 8 years old and 100k on a honda or toyota), you can generally find one for 1/3 of new sticker price. The first owner eats 2/3 depreciation, but had a shiny new car with a warranty.

If you drive it another 8 years and 100k, it's 2/3 used up, and you can sell it for about 1/6 of MSRP. That leaves you with 1/3 of the use for 1/6 of the cost, and still a pretty reliable vehicle. No warranty, but still respectably new and not too many mechanical issues.

By the time you sell, someone will get a deal on a beater which will have rubber parts starting to go bad, rust issues, and not be super reliable. It sounds like you're at that point with your Mazda.

You could buy a second car nearing the end of it's life and use it for a cheap backup. This has some good points, and some bad. You'll have two cars to license, insure, and maintenance, but added security.

You could sell yours while it's running good, and throw in some money to get a more reliable brand/model (even if it's the same age and mileage), or go for something a bit newer that's still in the goldilocks depreciation zone. How you go about it depends on what resources you have set aside. Ideally, you'd be able to take your time and get a good deal on something dependable, then not be in a rush to sell your beater so you can maximize your selling price.
